title: Precepts as Inner Work
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett's main teaching is that ordination as a priest is not about achieving spiritual accomplishment, but rather a commitment to practice humility, help others, and see everyone as Buddha. By embracing this mindset, we take responsibility for our own minds and efforts, letting go of the need to control or change everything. This approach allows us to cultivate mindfulness, curiosity, and playfulness in our daily lives, softening our patterns of mind and recognizing the interconnectedness of all things.

It seems like the root of precepts practice is a real inquiry into how it actually goes for us.
How do things work out?
What happens in our life?
Looking into patterns, triggers, habits.
Looking at what happens when we meet the world, which is always happening, moment after moment.

Some are complex.

Everything is always a little different than we think.
And so mindfulness practice, in its basic root form as remembering, seems to be a key ingredient to practicing with the precepts as investigation, as a way to learn.
To develop the quality of mind that can remember.
This possibility of actually snapping out of the dream once in a while.

They should act in the ways that I like.

A mirror in front of our generosity and our stinginess.
A mirror in front of our sexuality.
How do we act, and what is that reflecting?
What is that reflecting inside us, in our process?
What are we?
Who are we?

It looks inside.
It seems a deep kind of investigation.

They must be flaws in our fixed identity.

To soften around this radical oversimplification we do whenever we identify ourselves as anything or with anything.

It's a fuller responsibility than following rules, because it's taking responsibility for our own mind.
Not just what comes out of our mouth that somebody else can notice, or how we move our body.
So, taking responsibility for how we understand our own life.
While we can't control our life, we can take responsibility for our effort to study and understand.

Some curiosity.
Some interest.
Some playfulness.
And the great thing is that if we can soften around the idea that it's me, I'm that kind of person, we get some fluidity.
We get some new angles.
And so the invitation of this practice is to be willing to be with everything.
To notice the thoughts that arise moment by moment, even the fleeting ones, gone in an instant.
Not just the ones that stick and twist us up in knots.
You can't help but notice those, right?
And as you notice the thoughts and emotions and impulses that pass through mind, so many are negative.
Have you noticed this?
So many are a little difficult.
So many are a little threatening to some idea we might have about what kind of person we are or are supposed to be.
The judgmental thought.
The angry thought.
To notice that we want to drown them out with our narrative chatter, or to distract ourselves with entertainment and distractions, to stay busy.
It seems that you folks are willing to experiment with not doing that so much.
I don't know why you all have to be sitting around here.
To actually invite forward the states of mind that come and go, with equanimity.
To learn how not to be destabilized by the things we don't like, and how not to be destabilized by the things that we do like.
To turn towards everything and see it as best we can, as it is, not adding or taking away.
And what's great about this is it's not always so fun.
We don't always like what we see.
From our point of view of being the me we want to be, it's a little bit difficult to see all these judgmental thoughts or whatever it is.
But the good thing is that if we can allow ourselves to really turn towards this process, we start to notice also the gaps between the thoughts.
That the thoughts don't stick around.
That they change.
That they vanish again, and something new arises.
We can soften around these patterns and habits of mind so radically that they don't have so much hold on us.
Just an angry thought.
It's all it is.
And this is really powerful.
This is a great gift, for us and a gift for the world.
And we would never learn this unless we were willing to turn towards our experience this fully, this radically.
If we're always pulling away and not looking, we can't see the insubstantiality of these things, the softness, the spaciousness of them.
We could never see otherwise that what seems to be the opposite is in the middle.
Like we had a great teaching from the weather.
Did you notice while we were sitting it was sunny and raining at the same time?
So this is the nature of our life.
It's not this or that.
It's this and that.
Sunny and rainy.
Angry and tight and beautiful and generous at the same time.
In the middle of even the hottest, tightest of anger there seems to be also peacefulness.
Spaciousness.
Right there.
So to be ourself fully in our experience is to feel all of this, and to feel the way that it can coexist.
Which one is the real me?
If any.
If all.
As Dogen put it, to study the self is to forget the self.
Or maybe that means to just be with everything that's unfolding.
But sometimes these teachings of non-self can also confuse us.
There's a balance here.
The goal is not just to be like, "Ah, just being."
We're people in the middle of the soup.
We're in the action.
We have to make choices.
We have to respond.
Sometimes very quickly.
Sometimes not as quickly as we think.
But often we have to respond.
And sometimes we need a little willpower.
We need to actually just show up.
We need to make a choice.
Maybe we're ready.
Maybe we can do more than we thought.
Maybe we're stronger than we thought.
Maybe we can make a huge effort to wake up.
But maybe that effort can be a little more free.
Maybe it can be a great effort without strain, without tension, but effort nonetheless.
So there does seem to be a me operating in the middle of this [unclear: "non-menus"].
Other times the practice of non-self can be so freeing, if we can remember that it is available to us.
To recognize "anger is arising" is so much more spacious and free than something like "it pisses me off when you do that."
We can train our mind to see anger as anger, thought as thought, emotion as emotion.
We can remember, here's mindfulness training again, to turn towards all that arises with patience and curiosity.
And when we seem to violate a precept, we can wonder, "Now why did that happen?
That's interesting."
And then more thoughts arise around that.
We can wonder about causes and conditions.

To wind back the clock a little bit in our mind.
To wonder what choices did we make yesterday and the day before and the year before?
What influences came into our life that nudged us in one direction or another?

Maybe, as an example, who we're choosing to associate with.

When did I take that fork in the road?
Maybe I can remember next time.

The second set of three, the three pure precepts, are explicated and explained by the ten.

Do everything that increases awareness.

Number three, live for and with all beings.

Hold all precepts with restraint precept.

Embrace and sustain regulation and ceremony.

Anyway, this whole topic of precepts and conduct is known collectively as sila or shila in Sanskrit and Pali, the early Buddhist languages.
And there are so many lists of what the key ingredients of practice are.
One of the best, I want to bring up, is a great list of three: there are three ingredients to a healthy practice and therefore a healthy life.
This shila or sila, the precept practice, and then samadhi, and then prajna.

So precepts, and then samadhi means concentration or clarity, awareness, clear awareness or concentrated awareness.

So precepts, stable concentrated mind, and then prajna is translated as wisdom.

So now we're back to priests.
Priests don't necessarily know a lot of stuff.

Prajna means something more like insight or reflection or discernment.

Precepts, clear awareness and wise seeing.

Yes?

Tim?

If you want to take this on.

You can put your English name.
You can just skip that part if that seems a little self-conscious.
I don't want my identity in this.
But it's good to have your name in there.
*O Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, please concentrate your hearts on me.* Let's do it together.
*O Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, please concentrate your hearts on me.
I, Nomon Doan, Buddha's disciple, greet the new day with humility and joy.

May I today in all actions of body, speech, and mind affirm life, give generously, keep the mind clear, treasure the body, be courageous and kind in speech, open to and heal through strong emotions, and return to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha on every breath.*
Thank you very much.
